dims: Pi-Ramesses, at Qantir in the eastern delta
tx: Pi-Ramesses is fixed at Qantir by Bietak's mapping of the old Pelusiac branch of the Nile and the Austrian excavations; Tanis, the older proposal, holds only monuments moved there later. That the Bible's Rameses is Pi-Ramesses is the usual modern view; Saadia Gaon put it at Ain Shams.
Numbers 33:3-4 dates only the start, and adds that the Egyptians were burying their firstborn as Israel left, and that Yahweh executed judgments on their gods (promised in Exodus 12:12).

first month, year 1, month 1 (Exod 12:2); lamb chosen, year 1, month 1, day 10 (Exod 12:3); first Passover, year 1, month 1, day 14 (Exod 12:6); unleavened bread, year 1, month 1, day 14 to 21 (Exod 12:18); out of Egypt, year 1, month 1, day 15 (Num 33:3)
items.note: Rameses is where the march began, on the fifteenth day of the first month (Numbers 33:3); Raamses is also one of the storage cities Israel built (Exodus 1:11). Most scholars take it to be Pi-Ramesses, Ramesses II's delta capital, whose ruins lie at Qantir.

tx: Succoth is usually read as Egyptian Tjeku, the district at the east end of Wadi Tumilat. Kitchen and the Italian excavators put Succoth at Tell el-Maskhuta, while Naville, Petrie, Holladay and Redford take that mound for Pithom, and Gardiner rejected both.
Succoth in the Jordan valley (Genesis 33:17; Judges 8) is another place.
items.note: Succoth was the first camp out of Rameses (Exodus 12:37; Numbers 33:5). It is often taken to be Egyptian Tjeku in Wadi Tumilat, perhaps Tell el-Maskhuta, but that mound is also claimed for Pithom, so the site is only a proposal.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Succoth and the crossing of the sea, not at a place.
Egeria (late 4th century) was shown an Etham on her road to Clysma (Suez), but not where. Wikidata gives the item a point north of Suez with no source, so no site is drawn.
items.note: Etham lay “in the edge of the wilderness” (Exodus 13:20; Numbers 33:6), and Numbers 33:8 calls the land beyond the sea “the wilderness of Etham.” The place is not identified.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Succoth and the crossing of the sea, not at a place.

Egeria was shown Migdol and Pihahiroth on her road to Clysma. Wikidata gives the item a point on the shore south-west of Suez with no source, so no site is drawn. Baal Zephon has been put at Mount Casius by Lake Bardawil, north-east of Wadi Tumilat, and on the Gulf of Suez.

Numbers 33:7 has them turn back to Pihahiroth “which is before Baal Zephon” and encamp before Migdol; Exodus 14:2 has them encamp “before Pihahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, before Baal Zephon”. Numbers 33:8 shortens the name to Hahiroth.
items.note: Here Israel turned back and camped by the sea, before Baal Zephon and Migdol, and Pharaoh's army caught up with them (Exodus 14:2, 9; Numbers 33:7). None of the three places is identified.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between the crossing of the sea and Elim, not at a place.

Ain Hawarah, a bitter spring about 47 miles south-east of Suez, is the traditional Marah of the southern route (nineteenth-century travellers and surveys; Easton's Bible Dictionary, 1897: “probably”). Some propose Bir el-Mura, whose Arabic name is akin to Marah, and routes that cross further north put Marah near the Bitter Lakes. Ain Hawarah has no point fact, and Wikidata's point for biblical Marah has no source, so no site is drawn.
Numbers 33:8 calls the three days the wilderness of Etham; Exodus 15:22 calls it the wilderness of Shur. Numbers 33 says nothing of the bitter water.
items.note: After three days without water they came to Marah, whose waters were bitter until Moses threw in the tree Yahweh showed him (Exodus 15:22-25). Tradition puts it at the bitter spring of Ain Hawarah in western Sinai, but the place is not identified.

dims: Wadi Gharandel, an oasis in western Sinai
tx: Elim is generally thought to be the oasis of Wadi Gharandel, about 100 km south-east of Suez, on the southern route. Menashe Har-El proposed 'Uyun Musa instead, which Hoffmeier finds too close to the crossing.
Nineteenth-century travellers and the Sinai survey of 1868-69; Stewart (1857) has “Wadi Gherundel probably Elim”.
Numbers 33:9 keeps Elim's twelve springs and seventy palm trees, as Exodus 15:27 does.
items.note: Elim had twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and Israel camped there by the waters (Exodus 15:27; Numbers 33:9). It is traditionally placed at the oasis of Wadi Gharandel in western Sinai, which is not proven.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Elim and Dophkah, not at a place.
Often put near Abu Zenima, on the shore; no point is fixed.
Only Numbers 33 has this camp: Exodus 16:1 goes from Elim to the wilderness of Sin.
items.note: After Elim they “encamped by the Red Sea” (Numbers 33:10), a camp that Exodus does not mention. Its place is not known; on the southern route it would be on the shore of the Gulf of Suez, south of Elim.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Elim and Dophkah, not at a place.
The plain of el-Markha, on the Gulf of Suez, follows from the Jebel Musa tradition for Sinai; no point fact was found for it.
Numbers 33:11 lists it as a camp; Exodus 16:1 says they came to it on the fifteenth day of the second month.
“Sin, the stronghold of Egypt” (Ezekiel 30:15-16) is an Egyptian city, not this wilderness.
wilderness of Sin, year 1, month 2, day 15 (Exod 16:1)
items.note: The wilderness of Sin lies “between Elim and Sinai” (Exodus 16:1); there the people grumbled for food and Yahweh gave quail and manna. Where it lies depends on where Sinai is; tradition puts it on the coastal plain of el-Markha.

dims: Serabit el-Khadim, the Egyptian turquoise mines
tx: Some link Dophkah with the Egyptian word for turquoise and so with the mines at Serabit el-Khadim or Wadi Maghareh; the derivation is unproven. Easton's put it somewhere in Wadi Feiran.
Dophkah and Alush are only in Numbers 33: Exodus 17:1 goes from the wilderness of Sin to Rephidim.
items.note: Dophkah is named only in Numbers 33:12-13, between the wilderness of Sin and Alush. It is not identified; one proposal links the name to the Egyptian turquoise mines at Serabit el-Khadim.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Dophkah and Rephidim, not at a place.
Dophkah and Alush are only in Numbers 33: Exodus 17:1 goes from the wilderness of Sin to Rephidim.
items.note: Alush is named only in Numbers 33:13-14, the last camp before Rephidim. Its place is not known.

dims: Wadi Feiran, an oasis in southern Sinai
tx: The oasis of Wadi Feiran is the classic Rephidim of the southern route, argued by E. H. Palmer of the 1868-69 survey. Others propose Wadi Refayid in south-west Sinai, or, for those who put Sinai in Midian, a site north of al-Bad'.
Feiran is Byzantine Pharan, a monastic centre on the pilgrims' road to Sinai, where Egeria stopped; the Rephidim identification is the 19th-century surveyors'.
Numbers 33:14 keeps “no water for the people to drink” but leaves out the rock in Horeb, the names Massah and Meribah, and the battle with Amalek.
items.note: At Rephidim there was no water until Moses struck the rock in Horeb, and the place was named Massah and Meribah; there too Israel fought Amalek (Exodus 17). Tradition places it at the oasis of Wadi Feiran, which is not proven.

dims: Jebel Musa, above Saint Catherine's Monastery
tx: Jebel Musa is the Christian and Muslim traditional Sinai. Jebel Serbal, Jebel Katarina beside it, Har Karkom in the Negev and Jabal al-Lawz in Midian are among the others proposed; none is proven.
Egeria (late 4th century) found a church on the summit and monks on the mountain; the monastery at its foot was built in the 6th century.
Numbers 33:15 names only the wilderness of Sinai; Exodus has them encamp before the mountain, which it calls Mount Sinai (19:2, 11), and puts the rock in Horeb at Rephidim (17:6).

reach Sinai, year 1, month 3 (Exod 19:1); tabernacle commanded, year 2, month 1, day 1 (Exod 40:2); tabernacle raised, year 2, month 1, day 1 (Exod 40:17); altar dedicated, year 2, month 1, day 1 (Num 7:1); Passover at Sinai, year 2, month 1, day 14 (Num 9:5); census commanded, year 2, month 2, day 1 (Num 1:1); census taken, year 2, month 2, day 1 (Num 1:18); second-month Passover, year 2, month 2, day 14 (Num 9:11); cloud lifts, year 2, month 2, day 20 (Num 10:11)
items.note: In the third month they came into the wilderness of Sinai and camped before the mountain, where Yahweh gave the commandments; they set out again in the second month of the second year (Exodus 19:1-2; Numbers 10:11-12). The mountain is traditionally Jebel Musa above Saint Catherine's Monastery, held since at least the 4th century; scholars propose several others.
rg: The mountain: Mount Sinai, Horeb, the Mountain of God

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between the wilderness of Sinai and Hazeroth, not at a place.
Rueis el-Ebeirig, north-east of Jebel Musa (Palmer; Janzen). Wikidata's point for it is an arc-minute shared with its Hazeroth, so it marks no site.
items.note: The first camp after Sinai, where the people craved meat: quail came on the wind, and a plague followed. Its name means graves of craving. It is not identified.

dims: Ain Hudra, an oasis north-east of Jebel Musa
tx: The oasis of Ain Hudra is the long-held Hazeroth for those who put Sinai at Jebel Musa, from the likeness of the names. Those who put Sinai elsewhere place it elsewhere: Jarvis put it at Hadhira, under Jebel Halal.
Burckhardt (early 19th century), followed by most dictionaries.
Deuteronomy 1:1 names a Hazeroth among places in the Arabah over against Suf; most take it for this camp.
items.note: Here Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, and Miriam was struck with leprosy and shut outside the camp seven days. Tradition puts Hazeroth at the oasis of Ain Hudra, north-east of the traditional Sinai.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Hazeroth and Abronah, not at a place.
Wadi el-Rutmi or Wadi Abu Retemat (Janzen); the name means broom bush.
items.note: A camp named only in Numbers 33. It is not identified.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Hazeroth and Abronah, not at a place.
items.note: A camp named only in Numbers 33. It is not identified.

Libnah of Judah, the town Joshua took and a Levite city (Joshua 10:29-39; 21:13; 2 Kings 19:8), is another place.
items.note: A camp in the wilderness, not the Libnah of Judah that Joshua took. It is not identified.

Tara umm Haluf or Jebel Taret um-Basis (Janzen).
Terah, Abraham's father (Genesis 11:24-32; Joshua 24:2; Luke 3:34), is a person.
items.note: A camp named only in Numbers 33, not Abraham's father Terah. It is not identified.

Bir al-Hafir (Janzen); others put it near Mount Hor, to square Deuteronomy 10:6 with Numbers 20:22-29.
Deuteronomy 10:6 goes from Beeroth Bene Jaakan to Moserah; Numbers 33:30-31 goes from Moseroth to Bene Jaakan.
items.note: Deuteronomy calls it Moserah and says Aaron died and was buried there; Numbers puts his death on Mount Hor. It is not identified.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Hazeroth and Abronah, not at a place.
Jaakan the Horite (1 Chronicles 1:42) is a person; the name may mean the wells of his sons.
items.note: Deuteronomy calls it Beeroth Bene Jaakan, the wells of the sons of Jaakan, and puts it before Moserah, not after. It is not identified.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Hazeroth and Abronah, not at a place.
items.note: Deuteronomy calls it Gudgodah. It is not identified.

The spring at Sabkhat et-Taba in the Arabah north of Eilat, the only candidate with remains; Ein Ghadian by Kibbutz Yotvata, which took the name; or Bir Taba south of Eilat (Rothenberg). No point fact was found for any of them.
items.note: Deuteronomy calls it a land of brooks of water. It is not identified; springs in the Arabah north of Eilat and at Taba south of it are proposed.

dims: Avrona, by the spring 'Ain ed-Defiyeh, north of Eilat
tx: 'Ain ed-Defiyeh, a small spring in the Arabah 15-20 km north of Eilat, is proposed by those who put Jotbathah at Ein Ghadian; the site beside it keeps the name Avrona. Those who put Jotbathah at Taba place Abronah at the head of the gulf instead.
items.note: A camp in the Arabah before Ezion Geber, named only in Numbers 33. The spring 'Ain ed-Defiyeh north of Eilat, at the place now called Avrona, is one proposal.

dims: Tell el-Kheleifeh, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba
tx: Glueck dug Tell el-Kheleifeh (1938-40) as Solomon's Ezion Geber; Pratico's reappraisal (1993) found no 10th-century level, so it may be Elath or a later Ezion Geber. Petrie and Rothenberg proposed the island harbour of Pharaoh's Island, 12 km south-west.
items.note: The camp at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, beside Elath; later Solomon built a fleet here. Tell el-Kheleifeh, west of Aqaba, is the usual site, but its dating is disputed, and Pharaoh's Island off Sinai is the other proposal.

tx: The region's richest spring, with an Iron Age fort; the name lingers at Ein Qadeis, 8 km south-east

The narrative brings Israel to Kadesh twice: the spies come back “to the wilderness of Paran, to Kadesh” in the second year (Numbers 13:26), and “the whole congregation came into the wilderness of Zin in the first month” (20:1), in the fortieth. Numbers 33 names Kadesh once, at 33:36, after Ezion Geber: the second arrival. Deuteronomy 1:46 has them stay “many days”.
Wikidata Q60790475, as on the Land of Israel page
items.note: Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, the oasis on Canaan's southern edge. From here the spies were sent and came back; here Miriam died, Moses struck the rock at Meribah, and Edom refused them passage. Tell el-Qudeirat, by the region's richest spring, is the usual site.

tx: Josephus put Aaron's death on a high mountain by Petra, and the shrine of Aaron crowns Jebel Harun; but that peak stands inside Edom, not at its edge (Numbers 33:37). Jebel Madurah, north-east of Kadesh, and Ras el-Khorasha are the main other proposals.
Josephus (1st century), and the shrine on the summit.
Numbers puts Aaron's death on Mount Hor (20:22-29; 33:38-39), in the fortieth year; Deuteronomy 10:6 puts it at Moserah. Numbers 33:40 repeats the king of Arad hearing of Israel (21:1-3).
The Mount Hor on the northern border (Numbers 34:7-8) is another mountain.
items.note: On Mount Hor, at the edge of Edom, Aaron was stripped of his garments, which were put on Eleazar, and he died on the top of the mountain at 123. Tradition puts it at Jebel Harun above Petra, where a shrine of Aaron stands.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Mount Hor and Punon, not at a place.
items.note: The first camp after Mount Hor, named only in Numbers 33. It is not identified.

dims: Khirbet Feinan, in the copper district of the Arabah
tx: The name survives at Feinan (Eusebius's Phaino, the Roman copper mines), and Khirbet Feinan is almost certainly Punon (MacDonald, 2015). Known for the town; the camp may have stood near it.
items.note: A camp on the east side of the Arabah, at the copper-mining district of Feinan in Edom, where the name survives.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Punon and Dibon Gad, not at a place. It is drawn before the Zered, which Numbers 21:11-12 reaches after Iyeabarim.
'Ain el-Weiba, Khirbet Ghweibah, el-Husub, or 'Ayna north of the Zered (Janzen). There is no agreement.
items.note: The first camp Numbers 21 names after the bronze serpent, on the way round Edom. It is not identified.

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Punon and Dibon Gad, not at a place. It is drawn before the Zered, which Numbers 21:11-12 reaches after Iyeabarim.
On Moab's south-east border, near the Zered: 'Ayna on the King's Highway, Khirbet Ay south-west of Kerak, or Khirbet el-Medeiyineh (Janzen).
Numbers 33:44-45 gives the camp two names in two verses: Iye Abarim where they encamp, Iyim where they leave.
items.note: The ruins of Abarim, in the border of Moab, toward the sunrise. Numbers 33:45 calls it Iyim, and Numbers 21:11 Iyeabarim. It is not identified.

tx: Continuous name (Dhiban); the Mesha Stele was found there; excavated.
Dibon in Judah (Nehemiah 11:25) is another place.
Wikidata Q126716537, as on the Land of Israel page
items.note: Dibon, north of the Arnon, which the children of Gad built, hence Dibon Gad. It is Dhiban in Jordan, where the Mesha Stele was found.
ln: On the Land of Israel page

tx: Not identified; drawn in its order between Dibon Gad and the mountains of Abarim, not at a place.
Khirbet Deleilat esh-Sherqiyeh or el-Gharbiyeh, north of Dibon, or Nitl (Janzen).
Almon of Benjamin (Joshua 21:18) is another place.
items.note: A camp between Dibon and the mountains of Abarim, usually taken for the Beth Diblathaim of Jeremiah and the Mesha Stele. It is not identified; the ruins of Deleilat north of Dibon are proposed.

dims: Mount Nebo, the landmark the verse names
tx: Continuous name (Jebel Neba); Byzantine Moses memorial at Siyagha. Pisgah's 'top' is equated with it in Deut 34:1.
Wikidata Q680161, as on the Land of Israel page
items.note: The range at the edge of Moab's tableland above the Jordan valley, where they camped before Nebo. From this mountain of Abarim Moses was told to see the land and die. The dot marks Mount Nebo, which Numbers 33:47 names; the camp lay somewhere on the range before it.

tx: From Beth Jeshimoth to Abel Shittim (Numbers 33:49): drawn as a bar between them.
Moses speaks, year 40, month 11, day 1 (Deut 1:3); Moses dies, year 40, month 11 or 12 (Deut 34:5)
items.note: The last camp, in the Jordan valley across from Jericho, stretching from Beth Jeshimoth to Abel Shittim. Here Balaam looked down on them, Israel sinned at Baal Peor, the second census was taken, Moses died on Nebo above, and Joshua sent the spies.

items.n: Through the middle of the sea
dims: Clysma (al-Qulzum), at the head of the Gulf of Suez
tx: 'Uyun Musa, the springs of Moses. Springs on the east shore of the gulf, south of Suez, named for Moses: the landing of the traditional crossing.

Lake Timsah: On the isthmus, by Ismailia (Haynes, 1896). The Bitter Lakes: On the isthmus; Kitchen and Hoffmeier favour the isthmus in general. Lake Bardawil (Sirbonis): The lagoon on the Mediterranean shore (Schleiden, Brugsch). Nuweiba, on the Gulf of Aqaba: Ron Wyatt, Bob Cornuke and others.
Numbers 33 says only that they crossed through the middle of the sea; Exodus names the Red Sea and tells the whole crossing.
Across Suez Bay, from under Jebel Ataqa to 'Uyun Musa: where the tradition puts it, not a known place.
items.note: Numbers 33:8 says only that they “crossed through the middle of the sea into the wilderness”; Exodus calls it the Red Sea (15:4, 22). Tradition since at least Egeria (late 4th century) put the crossing at Clysma, by Suez, with the landing at the springs of 'Uyun Musa. The other proposals are below, and none is agreed.

items.s: an end of the plains of Moab
dims: Sweimeh, Jordan, near the Jordan's mouth
tx: Name kept at Khirbet es-Suweimeh (Eusebius's Bethsimuth); the mound itself is debated.
Wikidata Q110921589, as on the Land of Israel page
items.note: The southern end of the camp, near the Jordan's mouth at the Salt Sea; later a town of Reuben. Its name lingers at Sweimeh; the mound itself is debated.

items.s: an end of the plains of Moab
tx: Glueck's Tell el-Hammam, the chief Iron Age mound of the plains, is the usual view; Tell Kafrayn (Josephus's Abila) also proposed.
The valley of Shittim (Joel 3:18) is another, perhaps the Kidron.
Wikidata Q55634648, as on the Land of Israel page
items.note: The northern end of the camp, called Shittim, the acacias. Here Israel joined itself to Baal Peor, and from here Joshua sent the spies and set out for the Jordan.

items.note: At midnight, Yahweh struck all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, and Pharaoh said, “Rise up, get out from among my people.”
On the next day after the Passover, the children of Israel went out with a high hand in the sight of all the Egyptians, while the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn.
They baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought out of Egypt, because they were thrust out of Egypt and couldn’t wait.
They encamped in Etham, in the edge of the wilderness, and Yahweh went before them by day in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire.
Yahweh told them to turn back and encamp before Pihahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, before Baal Zephon.
Pharaoh’s army overtook them encamping by the sea, beside Pihahiroth, before Baal Zephon, and they were very afraid.

items.s: at the crossing of the sea
items.note: Yahweh caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all night, and the children of Israel went into the middle of the sea on the dry ground.

items.s: at the crossing of the sea
items.note: The waters returned, and covered the chariots and the horsemen, even all Pharaoh’s army that went in after them into the sea.

items.s: at the crossing of the sea
items.note: Moses and the children of Israel sang, and Miriam answered them, “The horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.”
They couldn’t drink from the waters of Marah, for they were bitter; Yahweh showed Moses a tree, he threw it into the waters, and the waters were made sweet.
There he made a statute and an ordinance for them, and there he tested them: “I am Yahweh who heals you.”
They came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water, and seventy palm trees: and they encamped there by the waters.
In the evening, quail came up and covered the camp; and in the morning, on the surface of the wilderness was a small round thing. “The house of Israel called its name Manna” (16:31).
On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, for “tomorrow is a solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to Yahweh.”
Moses struck the rock in Horeb, and he called the name of the place Massah, and Meribah, because the children of Israel quarreled.
Amalek came and fought with Israel in Rephidim; when Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and Joshua defeated Amalek.

Jethro came with Moses’ wife and sons “into the wilderness where he was encamped, at the Mountain of God” (18:5), and counselled him to appoint rulers over the people. Exodus tells it before Israel comes into the wilderness of Sinai (19:1-2); Deuteronomy 1:6-18 puts the appointing of the rulers at Horeb.
Yahweh came down on Mount Sinai in fire, and God spoke all these words: “I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”
When Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, Aaron made a molten calf.
In the first month in the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was raised up, and the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting.
Yahweh spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai: “Take a census of all the congregation of the children of Israel.”
In the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day, the cloud was taken up, and they went forward out of the wilderness of Sinai.

items.s: between the wilderness of Sinai and Kibroth Hattaavah
items.note: The people complained, and Yahweh’s fire burned among them; the name of that place was called Taberah. Numbers 33 doesn't list it; the narrative tells it on the way from Sinai, before Kibroth Hattaavah.
tx: Not at a camp: the mark stands halfway along the line between the wilderness of Sinai and Kibroth Hattaavah.

items.note: Yahweh took of the Spirit that was on Moses and put it on the seventy elders, and they prophesied.
A wind from Yahweh brought quails from the sea, and while the meat was still between their teeth Yahweh struck the people with a very great plague.
Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, and Miriam was leprous, as white as snow, and was shut up outside of the camp seven days.
The children of Israel traveled from Beeroth Bene Jaakan to Moserah. There Aaron died, and there he was buried.
From Gudgodah to Jotbathah, a land of brooks of water.
They returned from spying out the land at the end of forty days, to the wilderness of Paran, to Kadesh, and brought back word.
“Your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness… your children shall be wanderers in the wilderness forty years.”
The people stayed in Kadesh. Miriam died there, and was buried there.
Moses struck the rock with his rod twice, and water came out abundantly; these are the waters of Meribah.
Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, but Edom refused to give Israel passage through his border.
Moses stripped Aaron of his garments, and put them on Eleazar his son. Aaron died there on the top of the mountain.
The Canaanite, the king of Arad, fought against Israel; Israel destroyed their cities and called the place Hormah.

They traveled from Mount Hor by the way to the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom; Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole. The text tells it between Mount Hor and Oboth and places it at no camp.
tx: Not at a camp: the mark stands halfway along the line between Mount Hor and Oboth.

items.s: between Dibon Gad and the plains of Moab
items.note: Sihon would not allow Israel to pass through his border, and fought against Israel at Jahaz; Israel took all his cities, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and lived in Heshbon. Numbers 21 tells it after they crossed the Arnon and before the camp in the plains of Moab.
tx: Not at a camp: the mark stands halfway along the line between Dibon Gad and the plains of Moab.

items.s: between Dibon Gad and the plains of Moab
items.note: Og the king of Bashan went out against them, to battle at Edrei, north of this map; they struck him and possessed his land. Numbers 21 tells it after Sihon, before the camp in the plains of Moab.
tx: Not at a camp: the mark stands halfway along the line between Dibon Gad and the plains of Moab.

items.note: Yahweh said to Moses, “Go up into this mountain of Abarim, and see the land which I have given to the children of Israel.”
Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah; Yahweh showed him all the land, and Moses died there in the land of Moab.
Balak the king of Moab sent for Balaam to curse Israel camped in the plains of Moab, but he blessed them.
Israel stayed in Shittim; and the people began to play the prostitute with the daughters of Moab, and joined himself to Baal Peor.
These are those who were counted by Moses and Eleazar the priest in the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho.
Beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, Moses began to declare this law.
The children of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days.
Joshua the son of Nun secretly sent two men out of Shittim as spies, saying, “Go, view the land, including Jericho.”

items.note: In the third month after they had gone out of Egypt, on that same day, they came into the wilderness of Sinai, and there Israel encamped before the mountain (Exodus 19:2).

items.s: year 2, month 2, day 1 · Wilderness of Sinai

items.s: year 2, month 2, day 20 · Wilderness of Sinai

tx: The verse gives the first month but no year. Year 40 is inferred: from Kadesh they went to Mount Hor (Numbers 20:22; 33:37), where Aaron died in the fortieth year, in the fifth month (33:38); and Deuteronomy 2:14 puts thirty-eight years between Kadesh Barnea and the brook Zered.
items.note: The whole congregation came into the wilderness of Zin in the first month. The people stayed in Kadesh. Miriam died there, and was buried there.

Aaron the priest went up into Mount Hor at the commandment of Yahweh, and died there, in the fortieth year after the children of Israel had come out of the land of Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month. He was one hundred twenty-three years old (Numbers 33:39).

items.s: year 40, month 11, day 1 · Plains of Moab
items.note: In the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, Moses spoke to the children of Israel, beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab (Deuteronomy 1:5).

items.s: year 40, month 11 or 12 · Plains of Moab
tx: Not dated. It falls after Deuteronomy 1:3 (the eleventh month of year 40), and thirty days of mourning and the three days of Joshua 3:2 come before Joshua 4:19 (the tenth day of the first month), so it was in the eleventh or twelfth month of year 40. He went up from the plains of Moab (Deuteronomy 34:1).
items.note: Moses the servant of Yahweh died there in the land of Moab, one hundred twenty years old (Deuteronomy 34:7); the children of Israel wept for him in the plains of Moab thirty days (34:8).

tx: The month and day are stated. Year 41 is inferred: it is the first month after Deuteronomy 1:3 (the eleventh month of year 40), and Joshua 5:6 says they walked forty years in the wilderness. It is the same day of the year as the lamb was chosen (Exodus 12:3).
items.note: The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and encamped in Gilgal, on the east border of Jericho.

tx: The month from Joshua 4:19, with no other month between; year 41, as for 4:19.
items.note: The children of Israel encamped in Gilgal. They kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month at evening in the plains of Jericho.

tx: The day after the 14th (Joshua 5:10); year 41, as for 4:19.
items.note: They ate unleavened cakes and parched grain of the produce of the land on the next day after the Passover.

The Mediterranean, the great sea of Numbers 34:6.
In the WEB both gulfs are the Red Sea: the sea crossed in Exodus 15:4 and 15:22, and the sea by Ezion Geber in Numbers 21:4 and 1 Kings 9:26.
The modern name. The WEB calls it the Red Sea: Israel crossed it, by tradition, at its head, and camped “by the Red Sea” after Elim (Numbers 33:10).
The modern name. The WEB calls it the Red Sea: Ezion Geber stood on its shore (1 Kings 9:26), and Israel went “by the way to the Red Sea” to go round Edom (Numbers 21:4).
Drawn at its high water of about 1900. The southern basin is now dry.
Drawn by the towns on its banks, down the Damietta branch from the head of the delta.
The plains of Moab lie on its east bank, across from Jericho (Numbers 33:48-49).
Moab's northern border (Numbers 21:13).
Thirty-eight years after Kadesh Barnea they crossed it (Deuteronomy 2:13-14).
The land's south-western border (Numbers 34:5).
The modern name; the Bible doesn't name it. One of the proposed places of the crossing (Haynes, 1896).
The modern name; the Bible doesn't name them. Some put the crossing here, on the isthmus.
Ancient Sirbonis, a lagoon behind a bar of sand; the Bible doesn't name it. Some put the crossing here (Schleiden, Brugsch).
The land of Goshen, in the eastern delta, where Israel lived (Genesis 47:27).
Exodus 15:22 calls the three days after the sea the wilderness of Shur; Numbers 33:8 calls them the wilderness of Etham.
Numbers 33:8’s name for the three days after the sea.
“Between Elim and Sinai” (Exodus 16:1); where it lies depends on where Sinai is.
The wilderness before the mountain (Exodus 19:1-2).
Where the cloud rested after Hazeroth (Numbers 10:12; 12:16), and from which the spies were sent (13:3). Its bounds are not given.
Kadesh’s wilderness (Numbers 20:1; 33:36), on the land’s southern border (34:3).
Esau’s land, east of the Arabah, which refused Israel passage (Numbers 20:14-21).
The tableland east of the Salt Sea; the plains of Moab are its Jordan valley.
Where Moses kept Jethro’s flock (Exodus 3:1), east of the Gulf of Aqaba as most place it.
The land Israel was going to (Numbers 33:51).

tx: Mount Hor · Oboth · Iyeabarim · the valley of Zered · the other side of the Arnon · Beer · Mattanah · Nahaliel · Bamoth · the valley that is in the field of Moab · the top of Pisgah
items.note: The narrative leaves Mount Hor “by the way to the Red Sea, to go around the land of Edom” (21:4), tells of the bronze serpent (21:5-9), and then names Oboth (21:10). It has no Zalmonah or Punon. After Iyeabarim it runs the valley of Zered, the far side of the Arnon, Beer (the well), Mattanah, Nahaliel and Bamoth to the top of Pisgah (21:12-20), where Numbers 33 has Dibon Gad, Almon Diblathaim and the mountains of Abarim before Nebo; only Oboth and Iye Abarim are in both. The camp in the plains of Moab follows at 22:1.

tx: Beeroth Bene Jaakan · Moserah · Gudgodah · Jotbathah
items.note: Numbers 33:30-33 runs Moseroth, Bene Jaakan, Hor Haggidgad, Jotbathah; Deuteronomy runs Beeroth Bene Jaakan to Moserah, then Gudgodah and Jotbathah, so the first two are the other way round. Deuteronomy says Aaron died and was buried at Moserah (10:6), where Numbers puts his death on Mount Hor, several camps later and after Kadesh and Ezion Geber (Numbers 20:22-29; 33:37-39).

tx: the Red Sea · Mount Seir · Elath · Ezion Geber · the wilderness of Moab · the brook Zered · Ar · the valley of the Arnon · the wilderness of Kedemoth · Jahaz · Aroer
items.note: From Kadesh, where they stayed many days (1:46), they turned “by the way to the Red Sea” and encircled Mount Seir many days (2:1), then turned north (2:3), passing Esau’s children by the way of the Arabah from Elath and Ezion Geber (2:8), and went by the wilderness of Moab. They crossed the brook Zered thirty-eight years after leaving Kadesh Barnea (2:13-14), passed Ar, the border of Moab (2:18), crossed the Arnon (2:24), sent to Sihon from the wilderness of Kedemoth (2:26) and fought him at Jahaz (2:32). It names no camps, and it passes Ezion Geber going north, where Numbers 33 goes from Ezion Geber to Kadesh (33:36).

tx: the Red Sea · Kadesh · the other side of the Arnon
items.note: Jephthah’s summary: through the wilderness to the Red Sea, to Kadesh, where they stayed after Edom and Moab refused them passage; then round Edom and Moab by Moab’s east side, to camp beyond the Arnon, and so to fight Sihon at Jahaz (11:20).
From the fourteenth day of the first month at evening until the twenty first day at evening they ate unleavened bread; no yeast for seven days.
They left Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month and came to the wilderness of Sin on the fifteenth day of the second month.
tx: Worked out from two dates, not stated as a length of time.

items.note: Each prince offered on his day for the dedication of the altar, Nahshon on the first day through Ahira the son of Enan on the twelfth day.
tx: It starts on the day the tabernacle was set up (Numbers 7:1; Exodus 40:17). Whether the first prince’s day is the 1st or the 2nd is not said.

items.note: They came into the wilderness of Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt, and the cloud was taken up on the twentieth day of the second month in the second year.
tx: Worked out, not stated: about eleven months and nineteen days if Exodus 19:1 means the first day of the third month, about eleven months and five days if it means the fifteenth.

items.note: The children of Israel ate the manna forty years, until they came to the borders of the land of Canaan; it ceased at Gilgal (Joshua 5:12).
tx: It began in the wilderness of Sin, after the fifteenth day of the second month (Exodus 16:1, 13-15); the exact day is not given.

items.note: The children of Israel walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the men of war who came out of Egypt were consumed.
tx: Drawn from leaving Rameses to coming up out of the Jordan: forty years less five days.

After the number of the days in which you spied out the land, even forty days, for every day a year, you will bear your iniquities, even forty years. The forty years are the whole count from the exodus, which already includes the year and more before Kadesh.

items.note: When all the congregation saw that Aaron was dead, they wept for Aaron thirty days, even all the house of Israel.
tx: It starts on the day Aaron died (Numbers 33:38).

items.note: The days from Kadesh Barnea until we had come over the brook Zered were thirty-eight years, until all the generation of the men of war were consumed.
tx: Neither end is dated: they left Kadesh Barnea after the spies came back, in the second year or later, and crossed the Zered after Aaron’s death in the fifth month of the fortieth year (Numbers 21:4-12). Its ends are drawn dashed.

items.note: From the Red Sea they went three days in the wilderness of Shur and found no water, until they came to Marah.
tx: Numbers 33:8 calls it three days’ journey in the wilderness of Etham.

items.note: The people were sanctified today and tomorrow and made ready against the third day, when there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain.
Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days; the seventh day he called to Moses out of the middle of the cloud.
Moses entered the cloud and was on the mountain forty days and forty nights; at the end of them Yahweh gave him the two stone tablets (Deuteronomy 9:11).
He was there with Yahweh forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread nor drank water, and wrote on the tablets the ten commandments.
tx: Deuteronomy 9:18 and 9:25 (falling down before Yahweh forty days, “as at the first”) may be these forty days or another forty.

items.note: Aaron and his sons were to be consecrated seven days, and atonement made for the altar seven days (Exodus 29:37).
tx: Commanded here, and done in Leviticus 8:33-35. Not dated.

items.note: They set forward from the Mount of Yahweh three days’ journey, the ark going before them to seek out a resting place for them.
“You will not eat one day, nor two days, nor five days, neither ten days, nor twenty days, but a whole month.” The place was called Kibroth Hattaavah (Numbers 11:34).
tx: Numbers 11:32 has them gathering quail all that day, all that night and all the next day.

items.note: Miriam was shut up outside of the camp seven days, and the people didn’t travel until Miriam was brought in again.
They returned from spying out the land at the end of forty days, to the wilderness of Paran, to Kadesh (Numbers 13:26); it was the time of the first-ripe grapes (13:20).
It is eleven days’ journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh Barnea.
tx: A distance in days of travel, not the time Israel took.

items.note: So you stayed in Kadesh many days, according to the days that you remained.
We turned and took our journey into the wilderness by the way to the Red Sea, and encircled Mount Seir many days.
tx: The text gives no number; it falls inside the thirty-eight years of Deuteronomy 2:14.

items.note: The children of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days, until the days of weeping in the mourning for Moses were ended.
They moved from Shittim and came to the Jordan, and camped there before they crossed over; after three days the officers went through the middle of the camp.
tx: How these three days and the three of Joshua 1:11 relate is not said.

items.note: The text counts years “after they had come out of the land of Egypt”: the second year (Exodus 40:17) is the year after the exodus year, so the exodus year is year 1, and Numbers 33:38’s “fortieth year” is year 40. Each year is drawn from its first month (Exodus 12:2), twelve months of thirty days; the text doesn’t say when the year number changes.

Between the second year and the fortieth the text gives no date. They stayed in Kadesh “many days” (Deuteronomy 1:46) and encircled Mount Seir “many days” (2:1), inside the thirty-eight years from Kadesh Barnea to the brook Zered (2:14). Numbers 15-19 (the laws, Korah, Aaron’s rod) are told without a date or a camp. Numbers 33:18-35, the camps from Rithmah to Ezion Geber, fill these years; the list never names the first stay at Kadesh.

items.s: the end of the forty years
items.note: Joshua gives no year. The first month after Deuteronomy 1:3 (the eleventh month of the fortieth year) is year 41 in this count: the end of the forty years, forty years less five days after they left Rameses, not a forty-first year of wandering.
tx: From Deuteronomy 1:3 (the first day of the eleventh month of year 40) to Joshua 4:19 (the tenth day of the first month) is about 69 days. Inside them fall Moses’ death, thirty days of mourning and three days by the Jordan; their order and overlaps are not stated.
